questions.explain: Teams moving from vendor consoles to open-source tooling identify 15–40% invisible waste in the first 30 days — because row-level querying of their own telemetry beats monthly vendor rollups. The three layers: Layer 1 billing ingestion (Steampipe, Infracost, CloudQuery) tells you what you spent; Layer 2 database-internal statistics (Query Store, dm_exec_query_stats, dm_db_index_usage_stats — built into the engine) tells you why; Layer 3 correlation/dashboarding (Grafana, Prometheus) connects the two.
options: Open-source tooling surfaces 15–40% invisible waste in 30 days via a three-layer stack: billing ingestion (Steampipe/Infracost/CloudQuery) → DB-internal stats (Query Store, dm_exec_query_stats) → correlation (Grafana/Prometheus)
Open-source tools can't match vendor consoles
questions.q: What is the open-source cost visibility stack, and why does it beat vendor consoles?

questions.explain: Steampipe exposes AWS/Azure/GCP resources as SQL-queryable tables — you query your cloud account like a database; one inventory query commonly surfaces stopped instances still billing storage (a stopped db.r6i.4xlarge with 2 TB gp2 costs $230/month while producing zero work). It also exposes aws_cost_by_service_monthly / aws_cost_by_resource_monthly for programmatic cost trends.
options: Steampipe makes cloud resources SQL-queryable — surfacing stopped instances still billing storage ($230/mo for a stopped 4xlarge with 2TB gp2) and programmatic RDS cost trends by tag
questions.q: What does Steampipe do for database cost analysis?

questions.explain: Infracost scans Terraform plans and outputs cost diffs before anything deploys — e.g., db.r6i.2xlarge → db.r6i.xlarge shows -$949/month, -$11,388/year before merge. The PR comment integration automatically flags every RDS-touching Terraform change for financial review, preventing expensive configs from reaching production unreviewed.
options: Infracost diffs Terraform plan costs before deployment (e.g., -$949/mo on a 2xlarge→xlarge downsize) with automatic PR comments so expensive changes never reach prod unreviewed
questions.q: How does Infracost prevent unexpected database cost growth?

questions.explain: On Azure SQL, DTU consumption ties to logical reads and CPU: a query averaging 50,000 logical reads × 200 executions/min alone justifies an S3 ($150/mo) → P1 ($465/mo) tier upgrade, but finding it and adding a covering index eliminates the upgrade need — $315/month saved from one index. The weekly db_cost_analyzer.py pipeline automates this pattern: Query Store top I/O + CloudWatch metrics + instance metadata → concrete saving estimates posted to Slack.
options: A 50k-logical-reads query running 200×/min can force a $150→$465/mo DTU upgrade — one covering index eliminates it ($315/mo); the weekly analyzer pipeline automates Query Store I/O + CloudWatch correlation into Slack reports
questions.q: How does database-internal telemetry translate into concrete savings?

questions.explain: OpenCost (CNCF sandbox) ingests AWS CUR data and exposes Prometheus-compatible metrics consumed by existing Grafana dashboards — billing data flows into the same panels engineers already watch. Prometheus with sql_exporter (or the Windows exporter's MSSQL collector) provides the time-series foundation for alerting on cost-correlated metrics like physical reads (IOPS billing) and memory grants pending (pressure forcing scale-up).
options: OpenCost exposes CUR data as Prometheus metrics for Grafana, and sql_exporter/WIndows MSSQL collector provide time-series cost-correlated metrics (physical reads → IOPS billing, memory grants pending → scale-up pressure)

title: Open-Source Tools for Cloud Database Cost Analysis
